newsitem.title: USA: Weather keeps Dakota rail movement at a standstill.
newsitem.headline: Weather keeps Dakota rail movement at a standstill.

text.p: Blizzard-like conditions and sub-zero temperatures in the U.S. Northern Plains this week halted rail traffic in North and South Dakota and conditions had not improved significantly by week's end, railroad officials said.
As of Thursday, all operations on the Burlington Northern Santa Fe Corp.'s South Dakota and Yellowstone divisions had stopped until tracks could be inspected, the company said.
"Conditions really haven't changed much, so we're having the same problems today (Friday)," said Mike Martin, spokesman for Burlington Northern in Fort Worth, Texas.

Rail traffic was stopped between Sioux City, Iowa and Willmar, Minn. and between Appleton, Minn. and Milbank, S.D., as well as between Mandan and Dickinson, N.D., Burlington Northern said in a statement.
There was no fresh snowfall on Thursday or Friday, and track plowing was expected to continue until tracks were cleared, the company said.
Short line railroads in North Dakota have also been shut down by the winter weather, according to Steve Cunningham, rail planner with the North Dakota Department of Transportation in Bismarck.

"I have spoken with the three short lines in the state and they are having some very difficult problems," Cunningham said. "They are working constantly to reopen their lines, but they all said they were having extreme problems."
Cunningham said temperatures were still well below zero in North Dakota on Friday and rail crews in the southern part of the state had encountered snow drifts of up to 45 feet.
Although traffic conditions were improving in other areas, the stoppages were causing huge headaches for shippers.
Many grain dealers characterized this week's traffic problems as the worst they had ever seen.
"This is definitely more severe than it ever has been in previous years," one Minneapolis-based grain merchandiser said.
Spring wheat movement in the Northern Plains was completely shut down by the blizzard conditions this week.
Because no one could get grain to market, some farmers were upset about missing the opportunity to capture profits from a rally in spring wheat prices, Cunningham said.
"Some shippers are losing up to a 90-cent per bushel premium on the wheat," Cunningham said. "Once everything is up and moving that premium will certainly drop."
The rail transport situation in North Dakota could ease if temperatures move up past 30 degrees Fahrenheit as forecast, Cunningham said.
However, the warmer weather was expected to be accompanied by ice and rain, which could cause a whole new set of problems for the railroads, he said.
